case_name: Saraga v. Wellington (County) Board of Education
text:
Ontario

Supreme Court

Saraga v.
Wellington
(County) Board of Education,

Date: 1995-06-09

Mair Saraga

and

Wellington
County Board of Education

Ontario
Court of Justice (General Division) Sheard
J.

Heard –
February 28, 1995
.

Judgment – June 9,
1995.

S. Wayne Mundy, for plaintiff/respondent.

Guy W. Giorno, for defendant/applicant.

95-CQ-60201

1
June 9, 1995. SHEARD J.:– In an action
commenced in June 1990, the plaintiff sued the defendant for damages for
wrongful dismissal. In his statement of claim, the plaintiff said that he had
been employed by the defendant as a probationary teacher, commencing September
1, 1987, and had been wrongfully dismissed the following May.

2
In October 1990, on motion by the defendant,
the action was dismissed by Mr. Justice Speyer. In his reasons for
judgment, Speyer J. said that the exclusive recourse open to the plaintiff was
the grievance and arbitration procedures found in the collective agreement
between the defendant and the Wellington District Branch of the Ontario Public School
Teachers Federation. “In view of the fact that the plaintiff’s contract of
employment is based on the interpretation and application of the collective
agreement referred to above, this court is without jurisdiction to hear the
plaintiff’s claim for wrongful dismissal. Accordingly, the plaintiff’s action
is dismissed with costs if asked for.”

3
The plaintiff did not appeal the dismissal of
his action. However, by a statement of claim issued in August 1994, the
plaintiff brought the present action against the defendant board. In this
action the plaintiff asserts that his rights under
s. 7
and
s. 15
of
the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

have been infringed by the
defendant and asks for relief under
s. 24
, specifically, an order
reinstating him in his position as a teacher with the defendant board, and
damages in the amount of $1.5 million.

4
The defendant now moves for an order striking
the statement of claim and dismissing the action. The grounds asserted by the
defendant are that the facts alleged by the plaintiff fail to disclose a
violation of his rights under
s. 7
or
s. 15
of the
Charter
,
that
the claim is frivolous, vexatious, and an abuse of process, that the
allegations in the second statement of claim should have been raised in the
1990 action, and that the matter is now res judicata and cannot be relitigated.

5
As an alternative, the defendant asks that the
plaintiff’s jury notice be struck out.

6
The 1994 statement of claim is longer than the
1990 statement

of claim and includes new allegations, as well
as repeating, in identical language, several of the paragraphs of the 1990
claim. In the new statement of claim, the originally pleaded account of the
plaintiff’s hiring and firing by the board is the central thread, but
allegations are now pleaded which form the basis of the
Charter

claims.
In particular, the plaintiff now alleges that he was denied the right to file a
grievance or any other recourse to challenge his dismissal except for a
presentation he was permitted to make to the committee of the whole of the
board of trustees, in which he was restricted to less than ten minutes; that he
was subjected by the superintendent of the defendant board to coercive and
intimidating conduct designed to obtain his resignation under duress; and that
the termination of his employment resulted from discrimination against him by
reason of his ethnic origin and religion, he being “a Jewish person of
Spanish-Moroccan ancestry.” This discriminatory conduct he alleges infringed
his rights under
s. 15
of the
Charter.

7
The plaintiff claims that his rights under

s. 7
of the
Charter

were infringed because he was denied a fair
trial and impartial hearing, and by reason of the conduct of the defendant
through its agents and employees. This conduct includes, as well as the
aforementioned allegations, that he was treated by the principal of one of the
two schools where he taught “in a differential manner.”

8
In this motion Mr. Mundy cites
Weber
v. Ontario Hydro
(1992),
1992 CanLII 7499 (ON CA)
, 11 O.R. (3d) 609 (C.A.), for the proposition that the plaintiff can bring his
Charter

claims
to this court for determination.

9
In
Weber
,
a judgment of the Ontario
Court of Appeal delivered for the court by Madam Justice Arbour, the plaintiff,
an employee of the defendant Hydro, sued for damages for deceit, trespass,
nuisance, and invasion of privacy, and for a declaration that his rights under

ss. 7
and
8
of the
Charter

had been violated. These claims were brought
in consequence of the defendant, suspecting the plaintiff of malingering,
having hired an investigator to conduct a secret surveillance of the plaintiff
and his family and property. The plaintiff discovered the surveillance and the
union filed three grievances on his behalf. On motion by the defendant, the
plaintiff’s action was dismissed on the basis that the court had no
jurisdiction.

10
Arbour J.A. said that the motions court judge
was correct in concluding that a court does not have jurisdiction to hear an
action for damages for the tortious acts of an employer where those acts are
also arbitrable under the collective agreement. The grievances filed on the
plaintiff’s behalf made no reference to the alleged
Charter

violations,
but Arbour J.A. stated that civil courts are not precluded from, and should not
refrain from, entertaining an action based on the
Charter
merely because
the matter is arbitrable.

11
On the first-mentioned principle, Arbour J.A.
quotes [at p. 614] the statement of Estey J. at p. 720 of
St Anne
Nackawic Pulp & Paper Co.
v. C.P.U.,
Local 219,
1986 CanLII 71 (SCC)
, [1986] 1 S.C.R.
704:

“The courts have no jurisdiction to
consider claims arising out of rights created by a collective agreement. Nor
can the courts properly decide questions which might have arisen under the
common law of master and servant in the absence of a collective bargaining regime
if the collective agreement by which the parties to the action are bound makes
provision for the matters in issue, whether or not it explicitly provides a
procedure and forum for enforcement.” (Emphasis added [by Arbour J.A.].)

12
After discussing the principles involved,
Arbour J.A., at p. 620, says: “For those reasons, it is sound social
policy to curtail access to the courts by individuals who have equal access,
through their unions, to labour arbitrations. Assuming that they properly arise
in a labour dispute context, claims of constitutional violation should not, on
the other hand, be subsumed by the labour context in which they arose, so as to
exclude the jurisdiction of civil courts in favour of arbitration boards.”

13
The appeal of the plaintiff was allowed, to
let the matter proceed to trial on the
Charter

claims alone, with the
applicability of the
Charter
and any infringement thereof to be
determined at trial. “There was insufficient material before the motions court
judge to allow him to take a hard look at the facts and determine the question
of law” [at p. 621 O.R.].

14
The defendant’s argument that the action is
now res judicata goes hand in hand with the argument that the second action is
frivolous, vexatious, and an abuse of process.

15
In considering the res judicata argument, it
must be kept in mind that the first action was dismissed before it was even
pleaded to by the defendant, much less tried. It was dismissed, pursuant to the
principle stated in
St. Anne Nackawic,
supra, because the court did not
have jurisdiction to hear it. What was adjudicated was that the plaintiff’s
claim for wrongful dismissal could not be entertained by the court because the
exclusive recourse open to the plaintiff was the grievance and arbitration
procedures found in the collective agreement.

16
The plaintiff founds his action on the
allegations of
Charter

breaches as to which his first action is silent.
The authority of
Weber v. Ontario Hydro

makes it clear that, in
Charter

issues, the existence of a collective agreement does not exclude the
jurisdiction of the civil courts. Indeed, Arbour J.A. expresses the view that
Charter

rights being individual rights, “[t]here should be little impediment or
restraint to the individual’s right to seek constitutional redress in the
courts” [at p. 618] notwithstanding the availability of grievance
procedure in labour disputes involving a collective agreement.

17
Mr. Giorno argues that the plaintiff
should not split his case, and every issue or point that could have been raised
in the prior proceeding should have been raised, citing
Henderson v.
Henderson
(1843), 3 Hare 100 (V.-C. Ct.)
, and
Doering v.
Grandview
(Town)
(1975),
1975 CanLII 16 (SCC)
, 61 D.L.R. (3d) 455
(S.C.C.).

18
However, if the
Charter

issues had
been raised in the 1990 action, it would have been inconsistent with the
principles of law stated in
Weber

for the action to have then been
dismissed as to the
Charter
issues, for lack of jurisdiction.

19
While the second action, like the first, is
based on the plaintiff’s employment by the defendant, the second action is not
simply a recycling of the facts alleged in the first action. The plaintiff has,
in the second action, made allegations not previously made and asserted, for
the first time, that his rights under the
Charter

have been infringed.

20
In my view, the second action is entitled to
be looked at as an action separate from the first action and not to be
dismissed at the outset as res judicata, frivolous, or an abuse of process.

21
Mr. Giorno argues that the plaintiff’s
claim does not disclose a violation of either
s. 7
or
s. 15
of the
Charter
.

22
He cites
O.P.S.E.U. v. Northern College of
Applied Arts & Technology,
[1988] O.J. No. 136 (Div. Ct.)
, Reid,
Rosenberg and Campbell JJ. [reported at
28 O.A.C. 100
], and other cases for the
proposition that
s. 7
does not protect a person’s economic interests and
consequently dismissal from employment does not infringe
s. 7
.

23
However, the plaintiff does not frame his
second action as a claim for economic loss, even though the fact of his
dismissal is at the core of his complaint.

24
Mr. Giorno argues that
s. 15

applies only where the alleged inequality is one made by “law,” citing
McKinney
v. University of Guelph,
1990 CanLII 60 (SCC)
, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 229,
Douglas/Kwantlen Faculty
Assn. v. Douglas College,
1990 CanLII 63 (SCC)
, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 570, and
McCutcheon v. Toronto
(City)
(1983),
1983 CanLII 1629 (ON HCJ)
, 147 D.L.R. (3d) 193 (Ont. H.C.).

25
In
Weber v. Ontario Hydro
,
the
question was raised as to whether Ontario Hydro is governed by the
Charter
.
Arbour
J.A. described that as “an issue of some complexity” [at p. 621]. As has
been mentioned, she thought there was insufficient material before the motions
court judge to allow him to determine the question of law.

26
In my opinion, the same can be said here. I
do not think that a responsible conclusion can be reached on what can be
described (particularly as to the applicability of
s. 15
) as issues of
some complexity when the material essentially consists of only the statement of
claim.

27
I think the action should proceed to trial,
where all the issues can be appropriately determined. It may be, as
Mr. Mundy concedes, that there is some overlapping in the two actions that
might lead to penalizing in costs, or that some paragraphs of the statement of
claim might be amended, but those are not matters to be determined in this
motion.

28
Although I must refuse the first branch of
the defendant’s motion, I think the alternative request must be granted. This
is not a case in which the issues of fact or the assessment of damages can
appropriately be tried by a jury.

29
To begin with, the plaintiff asks for
declaratory relief, which disqualifies the action for trial by jury because of

s. 108(2)
10 of the
Courts of Justice Act,
R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43.

30
Mr. Mundy, in his factum, says that
there is a difference between seeking a declaration, which the plaintiff asks
for in paragraphs 1 (a) and 1 (b) of his statement of claim, and seeking relief
pursuant to a declaratory order. I am not able to perceive this distinction in
the context of s. 108.

31
In my opinion, what was said by Krever J. (as
he then was) in
Fulton v. Fort Erie (Town)
(1982),
1982 CanLII 2121 (ON HCJ)
, 40 O.R. (2d) 235
(H.C.), is applicable here:

I have come to the conclusion that the
reasons for dispensing with a jury in this case are indeed cogent. In my view,
the case raises questions, some of which may be properly categorized as mixed
questions of fact and law and one, at least, of which may be fairly categorized
as a question of law of some difficulty.

32
The second branch of the defendant’s motion,
to strike out the jury notice, is allowed.

33
Success on the motion being divided, there is
no order for costs.

Motion granted in part.
